body:
Charlie Rose runs real estate credit at Invesco Real Estate, and his central argument is that a lender should optimize for downside protection rather than yield — a posture he calls "credit over yield." In practice that means better sponsors, lower loan-to-value ratios, higher cash coverage, and tighter covenants, with pricing used as the competitive lever instead of leverage or structure. Rose says Invesco will originate well over 50 loans in 2026 and has already closed or committed more than $5 billion year to date, a record for the platform, driven by banks' retreat from real estate debt and a heavy refinancing calendar.

The episode title points at the credit-over-yield strategy, and that theme does carry the conversation, but the discussion ranges wider: why Rose refuses to lend on data centers, how a single office loan in the San Francisco CBD marks a cautious re-entry, how an asset manager's observation about zero tenant tours killed a Bay Area office deal, and how a hotel borrower's hardball stance during COVID ended a seven-loan relationship. Rose also covers portfolio concentration discipline after the 2022–23 correction, Invesco's AI adoption, the European opportunity, and standby portfolio facilities for aggregation borrowers. Ted is the host.

Credit over yield means winning on price, not on proceeds

Rose defines outperformance in his credit strategy as hitting the target return agreed with investors and then beating on credit quality — better sponsors, higher-quality real estate, lower advance rates, higher cash coverage, better covenants. The operational rule that follows is explicit: in the Monday morning pipeline call, the default is to lean in on pricing rather than on leverage or structure. Given the choice, Rose would rather win a deal by being more efficiently priced than by offering a few million dollars more in proceeds.

The stated hierarchy of objectives puts principal protection first. Rose says downside protection matters more than optimizing yield, and that if the downside piece is wrong, the yield becomes irrelevant. Underwriting is described as risk-based and broad, covering physical property risk, climate risk, insurance risk, market risk, and counterparty risk.

The return levers, in his account, come from relationships rather than auctions. Invesco lends to roughly 100 borrowers in good standing, and Rose says over 70% of the loans originated in 2026 will be off-market or preferentially sourced with those borrowers. Avoiding heavily bid auctions is what allows a "true win-win" — the borrower gets certainty of execution, flexibility, fair pricing, and a relationship; Invesco gets a fair yield without being ground to the last basis point.

"If I have my choice, I'm going to try to win business by being more efficiently priced than my peer, rather than winning business by offering a couple million dollars extra proceeds."

No data center lending: single-tenant binary risk and AI correlation

Rose calls this a controversial position and says Invesco has held it for the last couple of years and will continue to hold it: the platform is not lending on data centers. He acknowledges the temptation — immense supply of opportunity, interesting headline yields, exploding tech valuations — and then gives two reasons for declining.

First, binary risk. In hyperscale situations there is often a single tenant. That tenant may be investment grade today, but it is still one tenant, and Rose says it is unclear how reusable the space would be or what functional obsolescence looks like 5, 10, or 20 years out. There is, in his words, no alternative use. That conflicts directly with the credit-over-yield mandate to avoid binary risk.

Second, correlation. Rose argues real estate credit has historically shown very low correlation to most other asset classes — public fixed income, public equity, private equity, private credit, and real estate equity — making it a diversifier in both broad and alternatives portfolios. Because much of the investable universe now carries meaningful AI exposure, removing AI exposure from the credit portfolio helps preserve that low-correlation profile. He also says he does not think many Invesco investors want the firm investing in data centers, even if they are not thinking at that level of granularity.

Office is underwritable again, but one loan out of more than 50

Rose's framing is that office looms large in industry consciousness — tall buildings, shiny CBD towers, careers spent in them — while being a relatively small part of the institutional universe today. The value destruction after COVID, compounded by the rate hiking cycle, was, by his account, unprecedented in speed and severity for any single property type, worse than what regional malls experienced earlier in his career.

For much of the last five years Invesco would not touch office. The reason Rose gives is uncertainty: he says the thing he hates most as a lender is uncertainty, and it was very difficult to underwrite demand, rents, and values while most players sat on the sidelines. Today he considers office much more underwritable, at least the good assets, because buildings are trading and values can be pegged with better certainty.

Two structural challenges remain. Office is capital intensive — building out a new suite is expensive and must be repeated as leases roll, creating a high CapEx burden that weighs on returns. And office tends to have more GDP correlation and, in many cases, binary tenancy exposure. Invesco made one office loan in 2026 out of what Rose expects to be well more than 50 total loans. It was in the San Francisco CBD.

The underwriting process runs on internal disagreement, not just third-party reports

Rose describes a two-step investment committee. The first convenes before a term sheet is issued, because Invesco wants high certainty of execution once a term sheet goes out — he calls it extremely unusual for the firm to issue a term sheet and then fail to close. The second convenes after third-party reports arrive: MAI appraisals, physical property inspections with construction specialists checking roof, plumbing, and electrical, seismic studies in active zones, wind and flood studies in hurricane-prone markets, environmental studies, and property and background searches on borrowers for KYC, OFAC, and AML issues. If a third party surfaces a major surprise, Invesco goes back to the borrower to adjust proceeds or add structure; in a few cases the borrower renegotiated price or dropped the acquisition.

The distinctive part is who is in the room. Originators are supported by associates and analysts who run the same cash flow model the equity side uses, so the valuation is built as if Invesco were buying the property, and the firm forms its own view of loan-to-value rather than deferring to the appraiser. Equity acquisitions teams, equity asset managers, and credit underwriters all participate, and at investment committee each is expected to evidence engagement and support.

Two anecdotes show how that input changes outcomes:

Bay Area office. An originator called the deal a slam dunk because Invesco owned a well-occupied building in the same office park and the buyer's basis looked similar. The asset manager on that owned building said to slow down: no tenant had toured the building in 12 months, and demand had shifted to the other side of the submarket near the Caltrain station. Invesco underwrote more conservative rents, absorption, and occupancy, and lost the deal on price — even though backward-looking public market data supported the transaction.

Phoenix industrial. A repeat borrower's deal looked like a slam dunk on paper, with two Invesco-owned industrial buildings in the same submarket and healthy market stats. An asset manager with 25 years in Phoenix industrial, based in Invesco's Southern California office, said she would not do it, calling it the last-in-first-out building in the market. Two reasons: inferior truck parking relative to competing buildings, and a micro-location requiring three left turns off the interstate versus one left turn or right turns elsewhere. Rose frames the diesel-fuel and time savings as compounding over years, pushing tenants to the easier buildings first.

"We are looking for information that is unique and not publicly available. And there are a lot of information asymmetries in the private markets, generally speaking, and in private real estate specifically."

Concentration discipline hardened after the 2022–23 correction

Rose calls the commercial real estate correction of 2022–23 one of the three most severe in the sector since World War II. The lesson he says he took from it is discipline around concentration risk, and he is more sensitive to it in credit than he would be in an equity portfolio, where concentrated bets are more acceptable. The goal is that a black swan at a single asset does not significantly damage the portfolio.

Portfolio construction in credit is, in Rose's description, less sensitive than a total-return strategy would be. The priority is avoiding binary downside risks, then aligning exposure with the top-down convictions of the real estate equity business.

Borrower relationships are the win-win mechanism, and they get revoked

Rose's stated principle is that Invesco is a relationship lender in business for win-win transactions. When collateral runs into trouble, the firm generally gives borrowers more time if they show commitment to the asset, commit resources and attention to the business plan, and put capital into the deal. If they do not, Invesco moves quickly — Rose says the firm can typically exercise remedies and take control of a property in 60 to 90 days in most jurisdictions, and that the credible threat is often enough.

The COVID hotel example is the sharpest illustration. Invesco had six hotel loans at the time. Five of six borrowers either committed to keep funding and inject capital or asked for modest accommodations such as accrued interest. The sixth demanded that Invesco fully accrue interest for a year and fund taxes, insurance, utilities, and labor out of pocket while occupancy had fallen from 85% to two occupied rooms. Rose's answer was that Invesco would do it, but investors would need to share the upside if the firm increased exposure at a difficult moment. Invesco commenced foreclosure, obtained a liquor license so the two remaining guests could be served, and the borrower paid off in full in July 2020. Rose says he believes Invesco was one of the only hotel lenders paid off in full that year.

That borrower had done seven loans with Invesco and Rose says he still considers them friends, but the firm has not made another loan to them and has passed on opportunities to do so. The inverse also holds: borrowers who handled genuinely failed business plans the right way get leaned into again, which Rose describes as the entirely opposite posture from "you failed, so we won't lend to you."

Banks' retreat, $3T of maturities, and a Europe and beds-and-sheds tilt

Rose says 2026 will be Invesco's most productive deployment year, with over $5 billion closed or committed year to date, exceeding the prior record. Two themes drive it. First, banks have fallen from roughly 51% of the real estate debt market pre-COVID to about a third today, leaving a gap that debt funds and alternative lenders are filling. Rose sizes the asset class at $6 trillion, the fourth-largest fixed income asset class in the U.S. Second, an elevated maturity environment: he expects $3 trillion of real estate debt maturities over the next five years, and notes that 2026 sits five years after the 2021 peak in loan originations. More of Invesco's originations today are refinances than historically.
